idiom_name: Crow App + CROW_ROUTE table + before_handle/after_handle middleware
implementation_notes: Crow (like Drogon) provides the whole front controller: a crow::SimpleApp owns the socket, routes are registered in one table with CROW_ROUTE, and middleware classes with before_handle/after_handle form the shared chain - globally through the App template parameters or per route via CROW_MIDDLEWARES. What replaces the classic structure: the App object and its route table replace the FrontController and Dispatcher classes, and middleware replaces the decorated pre/post-processing methods. Hand-writing dispatch over Boost.Beast or Asio stays the alternative when no framework is acceptable, at the cost of implementing routing, error mapping and middleware ordering yourself.
pitfalls: res.end() short-circuits the request: no later middleware or handler runs, so a guard must set status and body before ending and must not end by accident.
With multithreaded() every handler and middleware runs concurrently; per-request state belongs in the middleware context struct, never in the middleware object.
Global middleware runs before route-local middleware and both in declaration order, so reordering the App template parameters silently reorders the pipeline.
Crow is header-only and compiled into each translation unit - heavy templates mean slow builds and long error messages, part of the real cost of using it as the entry point.
